title: Node.js Security Essentials
summary: Quick revision notes on securing a Node.js/Express backend: password hashing, sessions vs JWT, security headers, rate limiting, zod input validation, secrets management and dependency auditing.

chapters.title: Node Security: Mental Model and Layers
points: Defense in depth: no single control is enough; stack hashing, auth, headers, throttling, validation, secrets and audits
Never trust client input: every body, query, param, header and cookie is hostile until validated

Threat to control map: stolen DB -> password hashing; XSS/clickjacking -> helmet headers; brute force/DoS -> rate limiting; injection/bad data -> zod; leaked keys -> env secrets; vulnerable deps -> npm audit
Typical Express middleware order: helmet -> rate limiter -> body parser -> validation -> auth -> route handler
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do; they are separate checks

chapters.title: Password Hashing with bcrypt and argon2
points: Hash, never encrypt: hashing is one-way, so a stolen DB does not reveal passwords; never store plaintext or fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256)
Salt is random per password and stored inside the hash string, defeating rainbow tables; bcrypt and argon2 add it automatically
bcrypt: await bcrypt.hash(pw, 12) and await bcrypt.compare(pw, hash); cost factor 12 is a common default, each +1 doubles the time; input is truncated at 72 bytes
argon2: await argon2.hash(pw) and await argon2.verify(hash, pw); default argon2id is memory-hard, resisting GPU cracking, and is the OWASP first choice
bcrypt vs argon2: bcrypt is proven and ubiquitous but CPU-only; argon2id tunes memory, time and parallelism; use argon2id for new projects
Mistakes: using sync variants that block the event loop, comparing hashes with === instead of compare/verify, cost too low, logging passwords, returning different errors for bad email vs bad password

chapters.title: Sessions vs JWT
points: Session: server stores state (in memory, Redis or DB) and sends an opaque session ID in a cookie; logout deletes it so revocation is instant
JWT: signed header.payload.signature token carrying claims (sub, exp); stateless, the server only verifies the signature; the payload is encoded, not encrypted, so never put secrets in it
Comparison: sessions give easy revocation but need a shared store when scaling; JWT scales without a lookup but cannot be revoked before exp without a denylist
Cookie flags for any token: httpOnly (blocks JS access), secure (HTTPS only), sameSite=lax or strict (CSRF defense), plus maxAge; localStorage tokens are readable by XSS
JWT usage: jwt.sign(payload, secret, { expiresIn: '15m', algorithm: 'HS256' }) and jwt.verify(token, secret, { algorithms: ['HS256'] }); pair a short-lived access token with a rotating refresh token

Mistakes: long-lived JWTs, not pinning algorithms (alg none or confusion attacks), storing JWTs in localStorage, trusting decode() instead of verify(), session fixation (regenerate the session ID on login)

chapters.title: helmet, Rate Limiting and Zod Validation
points: helmet: app.use(helmet()) sets security headers in one line: Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options and removes X-Powered-By
CSP restricts where scripts, styles and images may load from and is the main XSS mitigation; tune with helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({ directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } })
express-rate-limit: app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 15*60*1000, limit: 100 })) returns 429 when exceeded; apply a stricter limit to /login and /signup
Behind a proxy or load balancer set app.set('trust proxy', 1) or every client appears as one IP; use a Redis store when running multiple instances
zod: const Schema = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), age: z.number().int().min(18) }); use Schema.safeParse(req.body) and return 400 with result.error on failure instead of throwing

zod strips unknown keys by default (use .strict() to reject them) and z.infer<typeof Schema> derives the TypeScript type; validate params and query too, and always on the server since client validation is only UX

chapters.title: Secrets in Environment Variables and npm audit
points: Secrets (DB URL, JWT secret, API keys) live in environment variables, never in source code or the Git repo; read them via process.env.NAME
Local dev: a .env file loaded with dotenv or node --env-file=.env; add .env to .gitignore and commit only .env.example with placeholder values
Production: inject secrets from the platform (Docker/Kubernetes secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, CI secret store), not baked into images; use different secrets per environment
Validate env at startup with zod (z.object({ JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32) }).parse(process.env)) so the app fails fast; rotate any secret that ever leaked, since deleting the commit is not enough
npm audit lists known vulnerabilities in dependencies; npm audit fix applies safe semver-compatible upgrades; --force allows breaking major bumps; npm audit --omit=dev limits to production deps
Run npm audit in CI and fail on high severity (--audit-level=high); commit the lockfile, use npm ci for reproducible installs, keep dependencies minimal and updated

chapters.title: Node Security Cheat Sheet
points: Hashing: argon2id or bcrypt cost 12+, async only, verify with compare/verify, never plaintext or SHA-256
Auth: sessions for easy revocation; JWT short expiry with pinned algorithm; cookies httpOnly + secure + sameSite
Hardening: helmet() first, express-rate-limit with tight limits on login, trust proxy behind a load balancer
Input and config: zod safeParse on body, query and params; secrets in env, .env gitignored, env validated at boot
Maintenance: npm audit in CI, npm ci with lockfile, rotate leaked secrets, same generic error for bad email or password
